title: Where it worked
hook: where did Stoic practice actually change a day?

segments.voice: Yesterday: thank the emperor, the notebook Marcus wrote to nobody. Your line was to himself, to us. Did you read your own line again before bed? Day six hundred ninety-three. The end of the week.

What would count as evidence? A runner can show a race time. A baker can show the bread. A year of Stoic reading has no scoreboard. Its evidence is quieter: a sharp remark someone didn't make, a night someone slept instead of rehearsing an argument, a loss met a little more steadily. Nobody hands out medals for those, and they're easy to forget by the weekend. So today we go looking for them on purpose, one at a time. Where did it actually work?
screen: `NO SCOREBOARD FOR THIS.` → `A SHARP REMARK, NOT MADE.` → `WHERE DID IT ACTUALLY WORK?`

segments.voice: First, the Stoics' own test. Epictetus was blunt about where progress shows. Not in how many books you've read, he says in the Discourses, but in what you do with your desires and fears, in how you meet the day. In the Handbook he gives the picture we met back on day 381: sheep don't bring their grass back up to show the shepherd how much they ate. They digest it, and give wool and milk. So the question isn't what you know about Stoicism. It's where the wool showed. Second, the evidence is small. Look back down the year at the tools: a reply delayed, from Stoic in anger. A worry sorted into two columns, from Stoic at work. The evening questions, asked kindly. The view from above, for a night when something feels enormous. These are tiny hinges. A door swings on them anyway. Third, be specific. A vague sense that it helped won't hold up on a hard day. A real moment will: a time, a place, what you would have done, what you did instead. Marcus wrote book one that way. Not my teachers were good, but from this one person, this one thing. Fourth, the week behind us. We chose three habits to keep, and one idea to leave. We reread our notes from the first day of the porch. We thanked a freed slave, a flawed courtier, and an emperor who wrote to himself. Today we gather the proof, in our own lives, that any of it mattered. Tomorrow, just as honestly, the other side.
screen: `THE TEST: WHERE THE WOOL SHOWED.` · `SMALL HINGES SWING BIG DOORS.` · `A TIME, A PLACE, A CHOICE.` · `A WEEK OF KEEPING AND THANKS.` · then, large: `IT WORKED HERE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the year scroll back, slowly. Don't look for a big transformation. Look for one moment. A reply you held back. A worry you set down. A loss you met a little more steadily. A morning you began with a clear intention instead of your phone. When one comes, stay with it. Where were you? What would you have done before? What did you do? If it worked, there, once, let yourself notice it. If nothing comes, that's worth knowing too. The bell holds the time.
Where it worked: one real, specific moment when Stoic practice changed what you did, the wool and milk, not the grass. Today's word.

Your line: it worked here. Write down the moment you found, in one sentence, with the day or place if you remember it. If someone asks what you got from a year of this, that's your answer. Day six hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism keep a journal and note specific moments when a principle changed what they did, as evidence of progress rather than knowledge.

Handbook 46: what they ate shows in what they give, and Epictetus wants the same of his students.
a vague sense that it helped is the best evidence
a specific time, place and choice holds up better on a hard day.

fork.setup: a friend asks what a year of Stoic practice actually did for you. what do you say?
options: I can explain the dichotomy of control
one specific moment I did something differently

fork.reveal: Epictetus would want the wool, not the grass: a real moment where it changed what you did.

trapdoor: what you thought: Stoicism works if you feel calm all the time.
what it means: it worked in particular moments, a reply delayed, a worry set down, and you can name them.

what a scholar hears: Epictetus places progress in the work itself, in desire, aversion and action (Discourses 1.4), and Handbook 46 pictures it as sheep giving wool and milk instead of showing their grass.

notes: Week-end look-back covers days 687–693 (what you keep, what you leave, a year on the porch, the three thank-yous, where it worked).
